lessonSearchText: learning, setting up your computer, and running the project a repeatable workflow with vs code, powershell, node.js, and npm, from the first folder to a local next.js server. start from zero: install vs code and create your workspace by the end, you will be able to explain and apply a verifiable vs code installation and creation of a first working folder by the end, you will be able to explain and apply an experiment log that preserves evidence a developer does not memorize everything: they build a map connecting a goal, a file, a command, and evidence. every experiment should answer one small question and produce a verifiable result. always separate the intention, the incoming data, the transformation being performed, and the observable result. this separation lets you predict behavior before running code and diagnose an error precisely. like a laboratory notebook: the recipe alone is insufficient; you record what was tested and observed. open windows powershell from the start menu. winget installs vs code without assuming it already exists; if winget is unavailable, download the official installer from code.visualstudio.com and enable add to path. read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. this habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding. before any command, note the current directory, target file, and initial state. these three anchors prevent changing the wrong project or blaming a new change for an older problem. in a real project, verify this mechanism with the browser, terminal, or devtools instead of assuming it works. observable evidence is more reliable than intuition. after the action, preserve the exact command, useful output, and your conclusion in a log. an error then becomes learning data rather than an opaque failure. finally apply the concept through one small isolated change, check the result, and revert if needed. short changes make cause and effect easy to connect. workspace root folder containing the project code, configuration, and history. hypothesis a testable prediction stated before an experiment. feedback loop short cycle between an action and evidence of its result. winget --version winget install --id microsoft.visualstudiocode --exact --source winget --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements $courseroot = join-path $home "documents\lecomax-academy" new-item -itemtype directory -path $courseroot -force for any feature, write the expected behavior first, change one thing, then compare the before and after states. this practice workspace prevents touching l’ecomax too early; lesson four opens the real folder only after checking package.json. evidence of success: vs code is installed and powershell shows a lecomax-academy folder containing the created markdown log. “winget” is not recognized. app installer is missing or windows is too old to provide winget. update app installer from microsoft store or use the official vs code installer, then reopen powershell. an experiment does not reveal which change fixed the problem. several files or commands were changed at once. return to the initial state and repeat with only one variable changed per attempt. create a log containing a goal, prediction, command, observation, and conclusion. run setup.ps1 one line at a time in powershell and read each result before continuing. open learning-log.md and add your prediction for the get-location output. run get-location, record the useful path, and conclude whether the prediction was correct. a markdown heading starts with #. the conclusion should explain what the output proves, not merely repeat it. core idea: learning means producing a prediction, a controlled experiment, and a verifiable conclusion. workspace: root folder containing the project code, configuration, and history. hypothesis: a testable prediction stated before an experiment. feedback loop: short cycle between an action and evidence of its result. academy-labs/00-tools/setup.ps1

learning, setting up your computer, and running the project a repeatable workflow with vs code, powershell, node.js, and npm, from the first folder to a local next.js server. navigate safely with powershell by the end, you will be able to explain and apply absolute and relative paths by the end, you will be able to explain and apply safe read commands before any modification the terminal always has a current directory; every relative path starts there, while an absolute path names the full location. a command acts on the target obtained after that resolution. always separate the intention, the incoming data, the transformation being performed, and the observable result. this separation lets you predict behavior before running code and diagnose an error precisely. the current directory is your position on a map; “..” goes up one street and an absolute path gives the full address. get-location answers “where am i?” and get-childitem answers “what is here?”. run them together before a path-dependent command. read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. this habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding. set-location changes only terminal context, not files. -literalpath tells powershell to treat path characters literally, which matters for spaces and apostrophes. in a real project, verify this mechanism with the browser, terminal, or devtools instead of assuming it works. observable evidence is more reliable than intuition. resolve-path confirms a target before reading or modifying it. this check is essential whenever a command can write, move, or delete. finally apply the concept through one small isolated change, check the result, and revert if needed. short changes make cause and effect easy to connect. current directory location used as the starting point for relative paths. absolute path complete address from the drive root. relative path address calculated from the current directory. $courseroot = join-path $home "documents\lecomax-academy" set-location -literalpath $courseroot get-childitem -literalpath academy-labs -name resolve-path -literalpath academy-labs\00-tools\learning-log.md inspect first, resolve the exact target next, and only then run a command that writes. you will reuse this sequence in l’ecomax to distinguish app, components, lib, and public without changing their files. evidence of success: you enter 00-tools, return exactly to the root, and read the log without changing any file. powershell says the path cannot be found. the relative path starts from a different current directory than expected. run get-location, then use resolve-path or a quoted absolute path. a path containing an apostrophe or brackets is interpreted incorrectly. a wildcard-aware parameter treats some characters as patterns. pass a correctly quoted string to -literalpath. produce a text map of the practice workspace without changing a file or depending on l’ecomax. enter lecomax-academy and confirm the root with get-location. list academy-labs and academy-labs\00-tools without changing directory. resolve the log, read its heading, and compare its relative path with the absolute path. get-childitem accepts -literalpath without changing directory. add -name for cleaner output. core idea: every file command depends on a target resolved from the current directory. current directory: location used as the starting point for relative paths. absolute path: complete address from the drive root. relative path: address calculated from the current directory. academy-labs/00-tools/terminal-practice.ps1

learning, setting up your computer, and running the project a repeatable workflow with vs code, powershell, node.js, and npm, from the first folder to a local next.js server. understand node.js, npm, and scripts by the end, you will be able to explain and apply the difference between runtime, package manager, and dependency by the end, you will be able to explain and apply the npm ci, npm run dev, and npm run build workflows node.js runs javascript outside the browser, npm installs the package tree described by package.json and package-lock.json, and an npm script launches a local tool in a reproducible environment. always separate the intention, the incoming data, the transformation being performed, and the observable result. this separation lets you predict behavior before running code and diagnose an error precisely. node.js is the engine, package.json the parts list, package-lock the exact blueprint, and npm the mechanic assembling everything. node --version confirms which runtime version answers in this terminal. an incompatible version can fail a project before your code is even read. read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. this habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding. npm ci follows package-lock.json exactly and suits a clean install; npm install may recalculate and update the lock when adding a dependency. the lock guarantees the same resolution on every machine. in a real project, verify this mechanism with the browser, terminal, or devtools instead of assuming it works. observable evidence is more reliable than intuition. npm run dev favors fast feedback and stays active, whereas npm run build compiles and validates production output. a page visible in development therefore does not prove it can be deployed. finally apply the concept through one small isolated change, check the result, and revert if needed. short changes make cause and effect easy to connect. runtime program that loads and executes code. dependency external package used by the project with a declared version. lockfile file recording exact versions for the entire package tree. winget install --id openjs.nodejs.lts --exact --source winget --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements node --version npm --version test-path -literalpath package.json npm ci npm run build npm run dev keep the lockfile, use project scripts, and read the first useful error instead of repetitive final lines. l’ecomax uses next.js; npm run dev provides the local url and npm run build checks routes, types, and rendering intended for vercel. evidence of success: versions print, locked dependencies install, the server announces a local url, and the build completes without errors. “node” or “npm” is not recognized. node.js is not installed or its location is missing from path. install an lts version, reopen the terminal, and verify with where.exe node. npm ci refuses because the lockfile does not match. package.json changed without a consistent package-lock.json update. review the diff; if the addition is intended, run npm install once and validate both files. start l’ecomax locally, identify the url, and stop the server cleanly. install node lts, reopen the terminal, and verify node, npm, package.json, and package-lock.json. run npm ci and then npm run build; continue to dev only if both finish without error. run npm run dev, open the exact printed local url, then return to the terminal and stop with ctrl+c. the server intentionally stays active after ready. if port 3000 is busy, next.js may offer 3001. core idea: node executes, npm resolves packages, scripts standardize commands, and the build validates production. runtime: program that loads and executes code. dependency: external package used by the project with a declared version. lockfile: file recording exact versions for the entire package tree. academy-labs/00-tools/setup-node.ps1

modules.title: Internet, HTTP, DNS, servers, and APIs
modules.summary: Trace a complete request from a URL to rendered data, including methods, status codes, headers, DNS, HTTPS, and JSON.
lessonTitles: From browser to server and back
lessonSearchText: internet, http, dns, servers, and apis trace a complete request from a url to rendered data, including methods, status codes, headers, dns, https, and json. from browser to server and back by the end, you will be able to explain and apply the mental model behind from browser to server and back by the end, you will be able to explain and apply a minimal implementation verified by evidence the client starts an exchange by sending a request describing a resource; the server computes an independent response containing a status, metadata, and a body. the browser then interprets that body to produce the page. always separate the intention, the incoming data, the transformation being performed, and the observable result. this separation lets you predict behavior before running code and diagnose an error precisely. like a restaurant: the customer orders precisely, the kitchen processes it, and the waiter returns a dish with information about its state. a url supplies protocol, host, port, path, and sometimes a query. the browser turns these parts into an http message instead of reading server files directly. read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. this habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding. next.js receives the path, selects a route in app, and runs the necessary server components. the resulting response is serialized and transported even when client and server share one computer. in a real project, verify this mechanism with the browser, terminal, or devtools instead of assuming it works. observable evidence is more reliable than intuition. network devtools show timing, headers, status, and body for every exchange. use this view to separate a network fault from a react display fault. finally apply the concept through one small isolated change, check the result, and revert if needed. short changes make cause and effect easy to connect. client program that sends a request. server program that receives a request and builds a response. response body content transported after response headers. npm run dev powershell -executionpolicy bypass -file academy-labs/01-web/request-response.ps1 curl.exe -i http://localhost:3000/ to diagnose a blank page, first confirm a request exists, receives a useful status, and carries the expected data in its body. reload the l’ecomax home page and observe the main document in network, followed by separately requested images, scripts, and data calls. evidence of success: curl prints a 200 line, content-type headers, and an html body; network shows the same exchange. connection to localhost is refused. no server is listening on the requested port. run npm run dev and use the exact printed local url. the document responds but part of the page is missing. a separate script, image, or api subrequest failed. filter network for failed statuses and inspect the first red request. trace the home document from curl to the network panel. open academy-labs/01-web/request-response.ps1 and predict the example output. reproduce the example in the exercise file without copying the solution. run the listed command, compare the expected result, and explain any difference. start with inputs, then follow one transformation at a time. use the first error message and indicated line as diagnostic evidence. core idea: a web page results from observable request/response exchanges, not direct browser access to server files. client: program that sends a request. server: program that receives a request and builds a response. response body: content transported after response headers. academy-labs/01-web/request-response.ps1

internet, http, dns, servers, and apis trace a complete request from a url to rendered data, including methods, status codes, headers, dns, https, and json. methods, statuses, headers, and json by the end, you will be able to explain and apply the mental model behind methods, statuses, headers, and json by the end, you will be able to explain and apply a minimal implementation verified by evidence http is a message contract: the method expresses intent, the path identifies a resource, headers describe the exchange, status classifies the result, and the body carries the representation. always separate the intention, the incoming data, the transformation being performed, and the observable result. this separation lets you predict behavior before running code and diagnose an error precisely. an envelope carries address and instructions, a receipt reports success or trouble, and the enclosed letter is the body. get reads, post creates or triggers, put/patch replace or modify, and delete removes; the server must still enforce actual semantics and authorization. read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. this habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding. 2xx statuses indicate success, 4xx a request or authorization problem, and 5xx a server failure. response.ok covers 200–299, but fetch does not automatically reject a 404 response. in a real project, verify this mechanism with the browser, terminal, or devtools instead of assuming it works. observable evidence is more reliable than intuition. content-type describes the sent format and accept the desired format. response.json() should be called only when the body actually contains valid json. finally apply the concept through one small isolated change, check the result, and revert if needed. short changes make cause and effect easy to connect. method http verb expressing the requested operation. status code three-digit number classifying the result. header key-value metadata attached to a message. npm run dev curl.exe -i -h "accept: application/json" http://localhost:3000/api/products?limit=2 node academy-labs/01-web/http-statuses.mjs handle network error, unsuccessful http status, and invalid body separately so the message and diagnosis stay precise. product routes should return json with a coherent status; the interface checks response.ok before building a grid. evidence of success: the response exposes status, content-type, and a json body; a non-2xx status produces an explicit error. code parses json and receives “unexpected token <”. the route returned an html error or redirect page. inspect status and content-type before response.json(), then fix the url or route. a 404 response enters the success path. fetch resolves its promise for received http statuses. check response.ok and throw an error containing response.status. write a robust fetch that separates json success from failed status. open academy-labs/01-web/http-statuses.mjs and predict the example output. reproduce the example in the exercise file without copying the solution. run the listed command, compare the expected result, and explain any difference. start with inputs, then follow one transformation at a time. use the first error message and indicated line as diagnostic evidence. core idea: method expresses intent, status classifies outcome, and headers make the body interpretable. method: http verb expressing the requested operation. status code: three-digit number classifying the result. header: key-value metadata attached to a message. academy-labs/01-web/http-statuses.mjs

internet, http, dns, servers, and apis trace a complete request from a url to rendered data, including methods, status codes, headers, dns, https, and json. dns, domains, ports, and https by the end, you will be able to explain and apply the mental model behind dns, domains, ports, and https by the end, you will be able to explain and apply a minimal implementation verified by evidence dns translates a stable name into routing information, tcp reaches a service on a port, and tls authenticates the server and encrypts the channel before http flows. each layer solves a distinct problem. always separate the intention, the incoming data, the transformation being performed, and the observable result. this separation lets you predict behavior before running code and diagnose an error precisely. dns is the directory, the ip address the building, the port the office number, and tls the identity check plus sealed conversation. an a record points to ipv4, aaaa to ipv6, and cname aliases another name. changes are cached for their ttl and therefore do not become universal instantly. read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. this habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding. localhost bypasses public dns and targets your machine; port 3000 selects the development server. in production, https normally uses 443 and the platform then routes to the application. in a real project, verify this mechanism with the browser, terminal, or devtools instead of assuming it works. observable evidence is more reliable than intuition. the tls certificate must cover the requested name and chain to a trusted authority. https protects transport but does not automatically make server code authorized or flawless. finally apply the concept through one small isolated change, check the result, and revert if needed. short changes make cause and effect easy to connect. dns distributed system resolving names into records. ttl duration a dns answer may remain cached. tls protocol authenticating and encrypting the channel. resolve-dnsname lecomax.com -type a resolve-dnsname www.lecomax.com -type cname test-netconnection lecomax.com -port 443 curl.exe -i https://lecomax.com diagnose in order: dns resolution, port connection, tls certificate, http response, then application content. the l’ecomax domain must point to vercel, cover the chosen www variant, and redirect to one canonical https url. evidence of success: dns returns a target and https responds with a valid certificate plus an explicit status or redirect. some users see the old site after a dns change. resolvers retain the old answer until ttl expiration. compare multiple resolvers, wait for ttl, and avoid repeated edits. the browser reports a certificate name mismatch. the certificate does not include the requested domain or subdomain. add the exact domain to the platform, validate dns, then let it issue the certificate. draw and verify the name → dns → platform → https → application chain. open academy-labs/01-web/dns-check.ps1 and predict the example output. reproduce the example in the exercise file without copying the solution. run the listed command, compare the expected result, and explain any difference. start with inputs, then follow one transformation at a time. use the first error message and indicated line as diagnostic evidence. core idea: dns locates, the port selects a service, and tls authenticates and encrypts before http. dns: distributed system resolving names into records. ttl: duration a dns answer may remain cached. tls: protocol authenticating and encrypting the channel. academy-labs/01-web/dns-check.ps1

failure offers recovery without blanking the whole page. evidence of success: four validated products appear in console.table, or an error containing the status precisely explains failure. an older response replaces newer search results. concurrent requests are neither canceled nor ordered. abort the previous controller before each search or compare a request identifier. the component crashes on payload.products.map. the response does not contain a products array. validate array.isarray and turn failure into a readable error state. load four products, validate their container, and display a controlled error. open academy-labs/01-web/request-lab.mjs and predict the example output. reproduce the example in the exercise file without copying the solution. run the listed command, compare the expected result, and explain any difference. start with inputs, then follow one transformation at a time. use the first error message and indicated line as diagnostic evidence. core idea: a reliable api client checks network, status, shape, and temporal relevance before using data. api: contract exposing operations and formats to other programs. promise: object representing a future fulfilled or rejected result. serialization: conversion of data into a transportable format such as json. academy-labs/01-web/request-lab.mjs

modules.title: Analytics, consent, and growth
modules.summary: Measure useful intent with little data, respect customer choice, and run experiments that protect quality.
lessonTitles: Read a funnel without inventing causality
lessonSearchText: analytics, consent, and growth measure useful intent with little data, respect customer choice, and run experiments that protect quality. design an event contract name events after user intent, define a small set of stable properties, and exclude identity, free text, and secrets from analytics payloads. build a typed view_product/add_to_cart event with a timestamp and no personal information, then prove the result with this exact signal: the same gesture produces the same name and schema in browser, pipeline, and report, with controlled version and timestamp. analytics is a decision instrument, not a copy of the customer: every collected property must answer a defined question and respect consent. in “design an event contract”, the concrete input is a stable add_to_cart event containing useful product identifier and value without email, phone, or free text. event taxonomy means: a shared convention for names, properties, and meanings of measured events. the model is complete only when you centralize a typed, versioned contract, minimize properties, and test payloads before changing dashboards and can observe that the same gesture produces the same name and schema in browser, pipeline, and report, with controlled version and timestamp. product measurement is like a car dashboard: a few reliable indicators help you drive, while recording every movement distracts and increases risk. here the part you will actually inspect is a typed view_product/add_to_cart event with a timestamp and no personal information; stop using the analogy if it obscures the technical boundary shown by the code. start by bounding this lesson’s case: a stable add_to_cart event containing useful product identifier and value without email, phone, or free
